name: Okenite
emotional: Brings a soft sense of safety
spiritual: Opens the crown and heart softly

Often kept nearby for quiet restful moments
summary: Okenite is a fluffy white zeolite that grows in cotton-ball puffs of silky fibres, treasured as a gentle stone of compassion, softness and calm.
intro: Okenite is one of the most whimsical minerals, growing in fluffy white spheres of fine, hair-like fibres that look like cotton balls or cotton candy. The fibres radiate from a centre and can be so soft-looking you want to touch them, though they are delicate and break easily. It forms in the cavities of volcanic basalt, most famously in the Deccan Traps near Pune in India, often alongside green apophyllite and stilbite. Some specimens show several puffs together, others have a single perfect ball nestled in green crystal. The contrast of soft white against glassy green makes dramatic and photogenic specimens.
history: Okenite was named in 1828 for the German naturalist Lorenz Oken, who made notable contributions to natural science. It was first described from Disko Island in Greenland, and other early sources include the Faroe Islands and Iceland. For a long time it was a rare collector's mineral, but large discoveries in India in recent decades made cotton ball specimens widely available. Because the fibres are so fine, samples are best left untouched. In the crystal community, okenite has become popular as a gentle, soothing stone, with its fluffy look inspiring links to softness and sensitivity.
meaning: Okenite is regarded as a soft, compassionate stone. Its white, cotton-like puffs are linked to purity and gentleness, and practitioners use it to support emotional sensitivity, kindness and calm. It is connected with the crown, third eye and heart, and used to encourage quiet meditation and a sense of safety. Many people are drawn to it when they feel overwhelmed or very sensitive, since it is thought to provide a cushioned, gentle energy. Okenite is also said to enhance intuition and soft, open-hearted awareness. Because it is so delicate, it is seen as a reminder to treat yourself and others with tenderness.
howToUse: Place an okenite specimen in a quiet corner, such as a bedside table or meditation altar, where it will not be touched. Look at its soft fibres for a minute before meditation, then close your eyes and picture a gentle cloud. When feeling overwhelmed, take a few slow breaths while viewing it. Avoid handling it, as the fibres break. In a grid, place it near the centre with apophyllite and selenite for a soft, light layout. Use it as a symbol of tenderness in self-care routines.
care: Okenite is extremely delicate. Avoid touching the fibres, since oils and pressure can flatten or break them, and never wash it or expose it to water. Dust with a very gentle puff of air or a soft brush if absolutely necessary. Cleanse by sound or by holding selenite nearby rather than direct contact, and charge under moonlight. Keep it away from strong sun and heat. Store in a padded, covered box or display case to avoid dust and damage.
identify: Genuine okenite forms soft, white, fibrous balls composed of tiny needles radiating from a point, often nested in or on green apophyllite, stilbite or quartz. Imitations include cotton wool glued onto stones, which look matted and uniform. Natrolite and mesolite can also form fibrous puffs but usually look more needle-like. Real okenite fibres are silky and slightly glassy under light. Reputable sellers describe the locality, such as Maharashtra, and disclose any repairs.
